title: Earth Spins 1,000 MPH. Why Don't We Fly Off? 🌍
description:
Earth spins about 1,000 miles per hour at the equator, so why don't we fly off into space? Gravity explained in simple words: how mass pulls on mass, why gravity is about 300 times stronger than Earth's spin, why the Moon is always falling, what causes the tides, and why astronauts float on the space station.

topic: Gravity Explained in Simple Words: why don't we fly off the Earth?
script: You spin a thousand miles an hour, every day, so why don't you fly off into space? The answer is gravity, and it's weirder than you think. Let's explain it in simple words. Here's the big idea. Everything with mass pulls on everything else. The Earth pulls on you, your phone pulls on your coffee, and you pull on the whole Earth too. Isaac Newton wrote this down in 1687. His rule has two parts. More mass means a stronger pull, and more distance means a weaker one. Double the distance, and the pull drops to just one quarter. The Earth is huge, about six trillion trillion kilograms, so its pull on you wins easily. That pull is what you feel as weight. On the Moon, which has much less mass, you'd weigh about one sixth as much. So, back to the spin. At the equator, you really are moving at about a thousand miles an hour. Spinning does try to fling you outward, like water off a spinning bike wheel. But Earth's gravity is about three hundred times stronger than that fling. So you stay put, held to the ground. For you to float away, Earth would have to spin about seventeen times faster. A whole day would last less than an hour and a half. And you don't feel the spin at all, because the ground, the air and you all move together, smoothly, like passengers on a calm plane. Now here's the wild part. The Moon is falling toward us, right now, and it never stops. Newton pictured a cannon on a mountain. Fire a cannonball slowly, and it curves down and hits the ground. Fire it faster, and it lands farther away. Fire it fast enough, and the ground curves away beneath it as fast as it falls. It keeps falling, and keeps missing. That's an orbit. The Moon does exactly this, falling around the Earth about once every twenty-seven days. The Moon pulls back on us, too. Its gravity tugs on the oceans, making a bulge of water on the side facing the Moon, and another on the far side. As Earth turns through those bulges, most beaches get two high tides a day. And astronauts? On the space station, about two hundred fifty miles up, gravity is still about ninety percent as strong. They float because they're falling, just like that cannonball, racing sideways at seventeen thousand miles an hour. They circle the whole Earth every ninety minutes. Here's the strangest fact of all. Gravity is by far the weakest force in nature. A tiny fridge magnet can lift a paperclip against the pull of the entire planet. Gravity only wins because it adds up, and never switches off. So the next time you jump, remember, you pull the whole Earth up toward you, just a tiny, tiny bit. Next time: what would happen if all the insects disappeared?
key_facts: Earth's equator spins at about 1,000 mph (1,670 km/h)
Gravity at the equator is roughly 300 times stronger than the outward fling of Earth's spin; Earth would need to spin ~17x faster (a day under 1.5 hours) to fling us off
Newton published his law of gravity in 1687 (Principia); pull falls with the square of distance
Earth's mass is about 6 x 10^24 kg; you'd weigh about 1/6 as much on the Moon
The Moon orbits Earth about every 27 days; Newton's cannonball thought experiment explains orbits as falling and missing
The Moon's pull makes two tidal bulges, so most coasts get two high tides a day
The ISS orbits ~250 miles up where gravity is ~90% of surface strength, at ~17,500 mph, one lap every ~90 minutes
Gravity is by far the weakest of the fundamental forces; a small magnet can lift a paperclip against the whole Earth
